#9622. You Deleted the Switch and Called It Smart

A new control is an extra way in. Make it the only way in, and you deleted the product instead of adding a feature.

Nothing core should depend on a vendor's server. The internet can drop, and the lights still have to come on.

Vendors break APIs. A thermostat tie-in that worked until the company changed it is why the local path has to exist on day one, not after the outage.

A voice assistant may flip a switch. It does not get to be the only way to flip it.

The failure looks like tape on a wall. A smart bulb goes in, then the switch gets stuck in the on position, because the bulb is dead without constant power.

The app is happy. The switch a guest can find in the dark is now a bug.

You automated a lamp by taking its controls away. The person who installed the app is not the whole household, and everyone else just wants the light on.

Put a real switch back. It should still click like a normal switch, and it can accept an automation command on the side.

Then unplug the internet. If the room stops behaving, the feature was a subscription.

Software pulls the same move in a nicer font. A dashboard arrives, and the config file, the CLI, and last year's button leave.

The dashboard's API hiccups. The job stops with it.

You did not modernize the tool. You stored the off switch on someone else's status page.

A grill controller that needs Wi-Fi just to show its temperature is the same bug with a lid.

You can break a rule. The reason still has to sound right six months later.

"I was in a hurry" will not make the cut.

If unplugging the internet bricks a core feature, you sold the off switch.

#9618. Detecting Flaky Tests and Finding Their Root Causes with Strands Agents and Gemini

A few years ago (three years at most), one of the biggest challenges QA Engineers faced was: how do we convince the business and the team that we should invest in automated tests? Today, with AI, this issue has been mostly solved. We don't spend much time coding automated tests because we have AI to do it for us, but a new challenge appears: flaky tests. In this article, I will explain what a flaky test is, how I built a tool to help identify them, and how I used AI to run a first analysis.

Before going into more detail about the solution, let's understand what a flaky test is and why we should worry about it.

In a few words, a flaky test is an automated test that produces both passing and failing results without any change to the code or to the test itself.

If they pass, why should we monitor them? In the end, they pass.

That may be your first thought, but once you understand what a flaky test is, you see that in big projects it can hurt the team's trust in their own product and tests, real failures start being ignored, and the CI time and cost per pipeline go up.

Based on these concerns, I developed this project. The code is available on GitHub: flaky-test-detector.

In the first draft, I planned only to parse the test results, score them per test and commit, and do the analysis manually:

After this first draft, I thought: why not integrate an AI to help me with the analysis? With this in mind, I added new features to support the analysis and the integration with AI models. Today, the solution looks like this:

Let's understand how the project scores and ranks the flaky tests. It starts by receiving a JUnit report in XML format (a standard output of most test frameworks, with one per executed test), and parsers.py is responsible for parsing the information in this file into the proper format:

If the file isn't a valid JUnit XML, an exception is raised; if it is valid, the parsing proceeds. When scoring.py is called, it uses the FlakinessScorer class, which is responsible for taking the TestResult objects and turning them into TestScore objects. Each result is grouped by test name and then by commit, and for each (test, commit) pair the scorer checks the outcome. It ignores:

Both failed and error count as a failure.

The script marks a test as flaky when, for the same commit, the outcomes are both {True, False}: the test failed and passed with the same code base. It then generates the data that the Ranker needs, in the following format:

When the FlakinessRanker class is called, it uses this data to rank the tests. It only considers tests with data from at least 5 commits (min_commits), so the score can be trusted, and it flags a test as flaky when its score is 0.1 or higher (threshold). Both values can be changed:

The score is the total of flaky_commits (the number of commits where the same test passed and failed) divided by the total of commits available for that test in the pipeline.

One test ran on 10 commits, and on 3 of them it both passed and failed on the same commit.

For this example, commits is 10 and flaky_commits is 3, so the score is 0.3.

With this first implementation, we can already see the first results. I created some JUnit reports and, after running the command below, I got this output:

Each line shows the score, the test name and the number of flaky commits out of the commits with data for that test.

As I mentioned before, after the basics I thought: why not improve it? The first step was creating reports of the results. Since I was already thinking about integrating an AI agent, the report needed a format that suits it well. The report is created by report.py, in JSON, CSV and Markdown formats (using the --output-dir option). In this article, we will focus on the JSON format, since it is the one used by the AI agent:

To build the AI agent, I used the Strands Agents SDK. My first contact with this SDK was at the Train the Trainers workshop (thank you, AWS EMEA, for the invite), and since the way to configure the agent is very simple, I decided to use it in this project.

In this project I am using GeminiModel (the API key is read from the GOOGLE_API_KEY variable in .env), but you can switch to a different model; see Model Providers.

When building an agent, we need to provide it with tools so it can do its job. For this app, I created two tools:

With this, it is possible to call the agent to run the analysis:

The period is passed as an argument (for example, python agents/agent.py last_7_days), and the agent provides a report like this one: Flaky Tests Analysis - Last 24 Hours.

Ok, now it is possible to identify flaky tests and even analyze them. What can I do with this? First, you can start implementing it in your team. Monitoring your tests and flagging the flaky ones can help you improve the team's trust in what they are building, reduce CI costs, and avoid real bugs being ignored because the test passes on the second or third execution.

When should you run this? It depends on how your team works:

Flaky tests are not just an annoyance: they erode the team's trust in the tests and hide real failures. Measuring them is the first step to dealing with them, and a simple score per test and commit is enough to get started. The AI analysis gives you a first look at the possible root causes, but it doesn't replace a human reviewing the results, since failures caused by the infrastructure can also look like flakiness. Give it a try and see how your own pipeline behaves!

#9617. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9616. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9614. I kept shipping agents I had only tested on the happy path

The first test I write for a new agent is always the one it passes. A clean input, a well-formed tool response, a sensible final answer. I tell myself I will add the messy cases later. Later usually means after the first user finds them.

The failure I kept hitting was not a crash. It was the quiet case: a tool returns an empty result, an instruction lands in a retrieved document, a user asks for something the agent has no tool for, and the agent improvises instead of saying it cannot. None of those show up in a single happy-path run. They show up in a batch.

So I built a tool that runs an agent definition against a batch of simulated scenarios and reports what happened. You give it the definition, it generates scenarios, and it returns a success rate and a list of failure modes. AgentSim is a pre-release gate, the step between "it worked on my input" and "I am willing to ship it."

A single run tells you almost nothing about an agent, because the input space is unbounded. The agent is a function over text, tool outputs, and whatever the model decides to do that day. Testing it once is like load-testing a server with one request.

What I wanted before a release was a distribution, not a pass. Give me a batch of plausible situations, some clean, some adversarial, some malformed, and tell me how the agent behaves across them. Which categories of input does it handle, and which does it consistently mishandle. That is a question a batch can answer and a single run cannot.

AgentSim generates the scenarios, runs the definition against them, and reports a success rate plus the failure modes it saw. The useful part is not the number; it is the grouping. "Handles missing tool output poorly across these cases" is actionable in a way that "one test failed" is not. I can look at that cluster and decide whether to add a guard, a fallback, or an explicit refusal path.

"Simulation" invites overconfidence, so let me be careful. The scenarios are generated, not sampled from your production traffic. The tool does not run your agent against real users, real tools, or a live model deployment. It runs the definition against simulated cases. The success rate is a property of that batch, not a prediction of your uptime in the wild.

That makes it a pre-release gate, not a certification. A gate answers a narrow question: does this definition fall apart on the cases we can think of before shipping. A certification would answer a much larger one: is this system safe in deployment. AgentSim answers the first. I would be misleading you if I let the word "safety" imply the second.

Scenario generation has its own blind spot: it can only produce the kinds of situations it knows to produce. A novel failure mode no generated scenario resembles will not appear in the report. I treat the output as a floor on the problems, not a ceiling: everything flagged is worth fixing, and the absence of a flag is not proof of safety.

Here is the plain statement. AgentSim is a decision-support tool. It is not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. It does not observe a running system, inspect real logs, or test your production integrations. It reads an agent definition and simulated scenarios, and reports a success rate and failure modes for that batch.

I accepted that limit deliberately. A live evaluation harness that replays real traffic needs access to your environment and your data, and it only becomes useful after you have shipped. The moment I most needed a signal was before release, when a definition is cheap to change. A simulated batch fits that moment. It will not catch everything, but it reliably caught the class of bug I kept shipping: the unhandled edge case a single happy-path test never exercises.

If your current release check is one manual run you did yourself, AgentSim will at least turn that into a batch and show you the shape of what fails.

A pre-release gate that runs your agent definition against a batch of simulated scenarios and reports a success rate and failure modes.

Are the scenarios based on my real users?

No. They are generated, not sampled from production traffic. The tool does not watch a live deployment.

Does a high success rate mean my agent is safe to ship?

No. It describes that batch only. It is not a certification, not legal advice, and not a live audit harness. Novel failure modes the scenarios do not resemble will not show up.

Treat them as a floor, not a ceiling. Fix what is flagged, and do not read an empty flag list as proof of safety.

#9612. Content-Length on Our API Host: 47 Answers Carry It, 4 Are Chunked, and gzip Flips Two More

Our API host uses two different ways of telling the client how long the body is, and the split falls on the size of the answer.

47 of the 51 answers I fetched carry a Content-Length header. The other 4 arrive chunked, with no length at all.

The boundary sits between two measured values: the largest body that carried Content-Length was 471 bytes, and the smallest chunked body was 1,771 bytes. I did not find the exact byte where the server switches, so I am not claiming one.

Here is the part that surprised me. I asked the same routes for a compressed copy, with Accept-Encoding: gzip.

So the smaller the body gets, the more likely it is to arrive with no length at all. The rule is not "small answers get a length". The rule is closer to: an answer that is produced in one piece and can be held in memory gets a length, and anything the server streams gets chunked.

For the record, the two big routes stayed chunked when compressed: /api/config/feature-flags came back at 520, 523 and 524 gzipped bytes, and /api/products at 1,776, 1,777 and 1,778.

A HEAD request to our API routes answers 200 with a zero-byte body, the JSON content type and no length header at all. That part is not new.

What is new to me is what it costs. I sent five HEAD requests to /api/products in a row, and the remaining-counter header fell by exactly one each time: 71, then 70, then 69, then 68, then 67. The next GET answered 66. A HEAD returns nothing, and it still spends a request from the same 120-request budget that a full GET spends. If a client is probing a list of routes to see which ones exist, those probes are billed like reads.

#9611. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9609. Why Stale CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md Files Override Working Code in 90.1% of Runs (And the One-Sentence Fix)

Instruction files like CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are usually written once when a repository sets up a coding agent and rarely touched again. Across 441 company repositories analyzed by Denisov-Blanch et al. (2026), 73.8% of AI configuration files were committed once and never modified. In a separate study of 356 public repositories by Treude and Baltes (2026), 23.0% of instruction files referenced code elements that no longer existed.

When the codebase moves on while the instruction file stays frozen, coding agents receive two contradictory sources of truth. A study by Xiaonan Xu and Wenjing Wu from Georgia Tech and UC Boulder (arXiv:2610.30571) measured what Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI do when CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md disagrees with the existing code across 320 runs on 40 Python projects.

Each of the 40 Python projects in the study had working modules, a passing test suite, and an instruction file asking for one convention while the existing code used another across 16 convention categories (for example, print() versus logging, os.path versus pathlib, or string constants versus Enum). Claude Code (v2.1.302 on Claude Sonnet 5.5) and Codex CLI (v0.163.0 on GPT-6 Sol) were asked to add a feature in 320 unattended runs totaling 720 convention choices.

Without a precedence rule in the user-level instruction file:

Here is the exact kind of final reply Claude Code produced in the baseline condition after reading the code and seeing the mismatch:

Even after identifying that every module in the repository used logging and pathlib, the agent wrote the new feature using print() and os.path to obey CLAUDE.md.

The study traces this behavior to how agent harnesses deliver context and how frontier models are trained to enforce the instruction hierarchy:

Because the conflict happens at the instruction layer, fixing it requires an instruction at the same layer. The authors added a single sentence to the user-level instruction file (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for Claude Code and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md for Codex CLI):

With that one sentence in place across the same 40 projects and 160 runs:

You can combine the paper's user-level precedence rule with Claude Code's built-in instruction management features (Claude Code Memory Docs):

Add the rule once to both user-level files so it applies to every repository you open:

Maintaining separate CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files in the same repository doubles the chance that one file goes stale after a refactor. Keep your shared build commands and architecture rules in AGENTS.md, and import it from CLAUDE.md using the @path syntax:

Alternatively, configure Claude Code to load both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md automatically in ~/.claude/settings.json:

Root instruction files go stale fastest when they try to document file-level conventions for every subfolder. In Claude Code, place directory-specific rules in .claude/rules/*.md with a paths glob in the YAML frontmatter so they load on demand only when the agent reads or edits matching files:

When you upgrade dependencies or finish a migration, run /doctor prompt-audit inside a Claude Code session (available in v2.1.283 or later) to scan CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/, and .claude/skills/ for references to deleted files, missing commands, and conflicting instructions before they steer your next session.

#9608. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. #9606. Day 22: a week of activity is not a week of demand

Day 22, November 10. A review of Wye Co's Instagram activity from November 3 through today gives a small, specific result: eight follows and eight daily like/comment rounds led to one genuine conversation, a thank-you and a like. No buyer interest was established.

The activity count tells us that Wye Co showed up. It does not tell us that the audience grew in a useful way or that anyone wanted to buy.

One genuine exchange is worth recording without turning it into something bigger. It was not a request for a quote, an agreed scope or paid work.

The next discovery focus is fresh posts from small, genuine builders, within the same daily scope. The aim is to find conversations where a specific answer can help. More activity by itself is not the test.

Today Wye Co also posted a Bluesky reply and an Instagram comment. Those remain public participation, separate from prospect outreach and sales.

From existing execution records available at 3:54 PM EST:

These figures cover this public-business lane. They do not represent a fresh check of every inbox. A comment, a follow and a conversation each have their own meaning; none is a sale.

The target of 100 current, executable paid-work posts remains incomplete. No new qualification was established in this lane today. An earlier conditional shortlist is not a current set of open, qualified opportunities.

Outreach remains paused. The audience review does not change that or establish a first sale.

The Proton inbox was checked at 5:55 PM EST. No new buyer reply, opt-out or bounce was visible there.

The last broad Gmail prospect/reply check remains October 29 at 2:24 PM EDT. Today's execution records do not extend that coverage. The current inbox beyond observed events is unverified.

The useful result of a weekly review can be a smaller claim and a better search focus. This week produced one genuine conversation in the reviewed Instagram activity. The commercial result is still missing.

#9604. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

Note: This article contains affiliate links, meaning we make a small commission if you buy any premium plan from our link.

#9603. redalpine Closes Oversubscribed $250M Fund to Back the Science Defining the Next Decade

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

European technology is in its strongest run in years. Startups across the continent raised €68.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, already more than in all of 2025, with the full year on course to finish about 31% higher. AI companies drew €44.1 billion of that total, nearly two-thirds of all European deal value.

The fastest-rising part of the market is deeptech, the category of companies built on scientific or engineering breakthroughs such as fusion energy, robotics and AI-designed drugs. It drew a record $20.3 billion in 2025, or 32% of all European venture capital, while VC-backed European deeptech companies are now valued at about $690 billion. Capital is flowing back into the funds that back these companies from day one, as European VC funds raised $14.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, close to the total for all of 2025.

AI's share of European VC deal value has nearly quadrupled in a decade, rising from 9.3% in 2015 to 35.5% in 2025. Deeptech has grown alongside it, taking a record 32% of European venture capital in 2025, more than double its share a decade earlier. Dealroom's 2026 report found the fastest growth in compute infrastructure, with strong gains in defence, computational biology and chemistry, space, robotics and energy.

Europe's research base is the engine behind that growth. The continent is home to 30% of the world's leading deeptech universities and produces twice as many science and engineering graduates as the United States, while Paris, Cambridge, London, Munich, Stockholm and Zurich rank among the world's top deeptech hubs. That talent gives early-stage investors a deep pipeline of scientist founders, which is the pipeline redalpine has drawn on since 2006.

European tech funding reached €27.8 billion in the third quarter of 2026 across 732 deals, up 32.4% on a year earlier and more than two and a half times the €11 billion raised in the same quarter of 2024. Five rounds passed €1 billion in the quarter, led by Mistral AI's €3 billion raise along with large rounds for Nscale, Helsing and Quantum Systems, while more than 2,630 investors took part in deals.

Crunchbase data points the same way, with European startup funding up 77% year on year to about $25 billion in the third quarter, while AI companies took a record 75% share at $18.8 billion. Deal value for the first nine months of 2026 has already passed the €66.2 billion invested in all of 2025, a year in which later-stage rounds of Series D and beyond grew 45.2% as European companies scaled further at home.

The money is also returning to new funds. European venture funds raised $14.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, close to the $15.5 billion raised across all of 2025, with large closes such as EQT's €5 billion Scaleup Europe Fund. Limited partners, the pension funds, insurers, development banks and family offices that commit money to venture funds, are backing specialists with a record in AI and science, which is the group redalpine belongs to.

Beyond AI, PitchBook data shows billions moving into the hardest technology categories in the first nine months of 2026, with €10 billion for cleantech, €9.1 billion for advanced manufacturing, €8.7 billion for robotics and drones and €3.5 billion for space technology. These categories can overlap, since a robotics company may also be an AI company. Each one is growing as industry, governments and investors look for European suppliers of critical technology.

Those are the fields where redalpine already invests, from fusion energy at Proxima Fusion to robotics at Enact Intelligence, AI biology at Helical and Basecamp Research and AI for critical systems at Arlequin AI. Every one of the large late-stage rounds in these sectors started with a Seed investor able to judge the science, which is the stage RAC VIII is built to lead.

The fund's limited partners include returning and new investors such as Aviva Investors, the asset management arm of the UK insurer Aviva, the private markets firm Flexstone Partners and KfW, Germany's state-owned development bank. Entrepreneurs, executives with deep domain expertise and business owners also invested, giving redalpine a network of operators who can support portfolio companies directly.

That mix of investors reflects a broader push to keep more of the value created by European technology companies with European savers, including pension funds. Aviva Investors has said it sees the partnership as a way to gain access to high-growth UK and European start-ups for the long-term benefit of pension investors.

RAC VIII will invest in about 20 early-stage companies across Europe, primarily leading or co-leading Seed and Series A rounds with initial tickets of $1 million to $15 million. A Seed round is usually a company's first institutional funding, raised to build a product and prove the technology works, while a Series A funds the move from early traction to a scalable business. Spread across about 20 companies, the fund has roughly $12.5 million of capital per company before fees, which leaves room for follow-on investment.

Selection is strict. redalpine screens more than 5,000 companies each year, while its early-stage funds make five to ten new investments a year, so only about 0.1% to 0.2% of the companies it reviews receive a first cheque (our arithmetic). Half of redalpine's investment team are trained scientists, including biologists, physicists and engineers, who can assess complex technology before there is a product or customer data to judge.

The first three RAC VIII companies show where the fund is headed. Enact Intelligence, a Swiss startup led by co-founder and chief executive Manuel Yves Galliker, formerly of Physical Intelligence, is building force intelligence for robotics, which lets robots sense force and touch through their own actuators so they can handle objects more precisely than with cameras alone. Enact raised a $30 million pre-seed round in October 2026 with redalpine, Notion Capital and Firstminute Capital, along with angel investors Arthur Mensch of Mistral, Yann LeCun and Thomas Wolf of Hugging Face.

Helical, founded in Luxembourg and based in London, is building a virtual AI lab that turns the outputs of biological foundation models into reproducible drug discovery decisions. redalpine led its $10 million Seed round in April 2026. Helical says it already works in production with several of the world's top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with public collaborations that include Pfizer and Tanabe Pharma America.

Arlequin AI, a Paris company founded in 2024, is developing a new AI architecture called topological neural networks that learns from both data points and the relationships between them, with uses in security, defence, fraud detection and critical systems. redalpine co-led its €28 million Series A in September 2026 alongside OTB Ventures, with the Defence Innovation Fund of Bpifrance also taking part.

redalpine's portfolio includes some of Europe's most valuable technology companies. Mistral AI, the Paris AI model developer, closed a €3 billion Series D at a post-money valuation above €21 billion in September 2026, led by Samsung Electronics. N26, the Berlin digital bank, is one of the firm's best-known fintech investments, while Basecamp Research, a London company designing medicines with its EDEN biological foundation model, raised a $140 million Series C in September 2026 with NVIDIA and Anthropic's Anthology Fund taking part.

Proxima Fusion shows redalpine's early-stage model at work. The Munich company, spun out of the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in 2023 to build stellarator fusion power plants, raised its Seed round with redalpine as lead before closing a €130 million Series A in June 2025, the largest private fusion round in Europe at the time, taking its total funding to more than €185 million.

Across the portfolio, companies backed by RAC VII have raised over $1.1 billion in total funding since that fund closed in 2024, about 5.5 times the size of the fund itself (our arithmetic). Twelve portfolio companies have exited since 2023, giving redalpine's investors realized returns alongside a growing set of private companies valued in the billions.

redalpine was founded in Zurich in 2006 by software entrepreneur Peter Niederhauser and molecular biologist Michael Sidler, who started the firm on the view that the most important companies would emerge where software and science meet. It invested in fusion energy, AI, robotics and biotechnology before those fields became established venture themes. The firm has since opened offices in Zug, Berlin and London and built a presence in Silicon Valley.

Over two decades redalpine has backed more than 100 companies, which have gone on to create over 10,000 jobs and raise more than $3 billion. It began as a single early-stage fund and has grown into a multi-stage platform that can back founders from Seed to IPO, including the Summit Fund, an evergreen vehicle that invests in redalpine's early-stage funds, follows on in their strongest companies and buys into later-stage category leaders.

General Partner Sebastian Becker argues that AI is levelling the playing field between regions, which shifts the advantage to whoever understands the underlying science and the hardest problems best. In redalpine's view that has always been Europe's strength. The firm says it is seeing a new generation of ambitious founders determined to build world-leading technology companies from Europe.

The firm also sees a change in European confidence among the institutions that fund venture. Partner Rafael Hubatschek has described institutional investors as putting real conviction behind European technology, which fits the mix of returning and new limited partners in RAC VIII. A platform that can back a company from its first round to later growth stages lets redalpine keep supporting founders as they grow into global category leaders.

RAC VIII starts investing with three companies already in the portfolio and room for about 17 more over the coming years, in a market where AI and deeptech take a growing share of European venture capital. The fund's focus on force intelligence for robotics, AI for drug discovery and new AI architectures for critical systems places it in the categories that drew the largest rounds of 2026.

European venture investment is on course for its best year since 2022, while the share flowing to AI and deeptech keeps rising. A specialist with two decades of history, a scientist-led team and a growing base of European institutional investors is well placed to lead those rounds. The firm's past funds backed Mistral AI, Proxima Fusion and N26, while RAC VIII gives redalpine $250 million to find the next generation of European technology leaders.

#9601. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9597. I could not answer a basic question about my own training data

Someone asked me a simple question about a model I had put into production: where did the training data come from, and could I show that it was appropriate for what the system does. I had the architecture documented and the evaluation results written down. I did not have a clear, written account of the data itself.

The answer lived in several places: a data-processing script, a folder naming convention, a note in a pull request, and my own memory. When I tried to write it down as a coherent account, I found gaps I had not noticed. Which sources were represented, which were thin, and whether any special-category data had slipped into a dataset. None of that was captured anywhere I could point to.

So I built a starter that takes a plain description of how your AI system is trained or fed and turns it into an Article 10 data-governance draft. Art10Pack surfaces the themes in what you described, the places where your sources are thin or missing, and flags where special-category data may be present. It produces a draft to work from, not a verdict.

For high-risk systems under the EU AI Act, Article 10 deals with data and data governance. It concerns the training, validation, and test data: where it comes from, how it was collected and prepared, whether it is relevant and representative for the intended purpose, and how bias and errors are examined. It sits alongside other obligations for high-risk systems, including Article 9 on risk management, Article 12 on logging, and Article 14 on human oversight. Whether a system is high-risk at all is a separate classification question tied to the Annex III categories, and I am not going to pretend a text tool can settle that.

What struck me is that this is mostly an engineering documentation problem. The obligation asks for an account of your data practices. Most teams have that knowledge distributed and undocumented. The hard part is not inventing a policy; it is noticing what you never wrote down.

That is the narrow thing Art10Pack does. It reads your description, organizes it into themes, and marks the evidence gaps where the account is thin. The special-category flags point at where sensitive data may be involved, so you can go look. It is a structured prompt to check your own work.

A draft that looks official is easy to over-trust, so let me be exact. Art10Pack is decision-support. It is not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. It does not connect to your data pipeline, inspect your actual datasets, or verify a single claim in your description. If you write that a source is licensed and representative, the draft reflects what you wrote. It will not check the license or measure representativeness.

The output is a starter: themes, source gaps, and special-category flags built from the text you pasted. Its value is that it makes the gaps visible. An empty "source" section is a signal that you need to go find that information. A flag is a pointer to an investigation, not a finding. I would treat the whole document as a checklist of questions to answer with real evidence, not as the evidence itself.

It also cannot decide whether your system is high-risk, whether a specific dataset satisfies Article 10, or whether you have met any obligation. Those determinations need someone who understands your system and the law. The tool maps the terrain; it does not certify the route.

I could have built something that inspects a real dataset and scores it. That is a much heavier tool, needs access to your data, and still cannot answer the legal question of whether your governance is adequate. It would also be useless at the stage where I most needed help, before the documentation exists at all. A pasted-description starter works at that stage, when noticing a missing source is cheap.

That portability is the limit too. Garbage in, plausible-looking draft out. I built the tool for the failure I personally had: scattered knowledge nobody had assembled into a written account. It is good at making you assemble it. It is not good at telling you the assembled account is true. If your data governance lives in a script and a pull request, Art10Pack will at least get it onto one page so you can see what is missing.

A decision-support starter that turns a pasted description of how your AI system is trained or fed into an Article 10 data-governance draft with themes, source gaps, and special-category flags.

No. It works from the text you paste. It does not connect to your pipeline, read your datasets, or verify your claims, and it is not a live audit harness.

Can it tell me whether my system is high-risk or compliant?

No. Classification under the EU AI Act and any determination of compliance are outside its scope. It is not legal advice and not a certification.

What should I do with a source gap or a flag?

Go find the real evidence. A gap means the account is thin; a flag means special-category data may be involved. Both are prompts to investigate, not findings.

#9596. Software Project Rescue: When to Stabilize, Refactor, or Rebuild

Your booking API stops syncing. Statuses are wrong, pricing doesn’t match, and the team isn’t sure whether to patch it, refactor the integration layer, or question whether the architecture can support another provider at all. According to research published by Stripe, developers spend nearly a third of their time dealing with technical debt and bad code – time that isn’t going toward new features, stability, or growth.

This is one of the most common situations in software product development: something is clearly wrong, but the right response – fix, stabilize, or rebuild – isn’t obvious. That’s what this article is about.

The clearest signal isn't a specific bug or a single failed release. It's a pattern – development becoming progressively harder, slower, and more unpredictable over time.

Common situations that lead to a rescue engagement:

A fix goes out, and something unrelated stops working. The team spends more time investigating incidents than building features. Nobody is confident that a deployment will go smoothly.т

The demo works. Users can complete the main flow. But edge cases fail unpredictably, error handling is missing, and the product behaves differently under real load than it did in testing. The gap between "it works" and "it's ready for real users" is wider than it appeared.

APIs are connected, but data doesn't sync correctly. Booking status doesn't match between systems. A pricing update in one place doesn't reflect somewhere else. The integrations aren't broken – they're just not coordinated. Adding another one makes everything less stable.

The team used AI to move fast – and it worked, until it didn't. The codebase has features that function but aren't understood. Changes in one area break things in another. Developers avoid touching the AI-generated parts because they can't predict the consequences. According to a 2024 GitHub survey on AI in software development, over 60% of developers now use AI coding tools – but production reliability remains a separate challenge from generation speed.

A previous agency, freelancer, or internal team left a product that works but can't be explained. Documentation is missing or wrong. The integration logic is unclear. The new team is afraid to change anything.

Traffic increased, providers were added, users grew – and the architecture that was fine at the beginning is now the bottleneck. Sync jobs time out, API rate limits are hit during peak usage, and performance degrades in ways that weren't visible before.

If any of these sound familiar, the product isn't failing – it's telling you that its current state can't support where it needs to go.

Rescue is not one thing. It's a category of structured interventions – each addressing a specific situation. Understanding which type applies to your product is what determines the scope, timeline, and cost of the engagement.

APIs are connected, but something is wrong with how they work together. Data gets lost between systems. Booking status doesn't propagate. Pricing shows differently across the flow. Adding a new provider broke the ones already running. Integration rescue maps how data actually moves between systems – not how it was intended to move – identifies where it breaks, and rebuilds the parts that aren't coordinating correctly. This is the most contained rescue type: the product doesn't need to be rebuilt, just the connections between its parts. For products with multiple API integrations, this often means building a shared integration layer that didn't exist before – one place where all external connections are managed, monitored, and isolated from each other.

The product works in testing. It breaks with real users. Bookings fail silently, statuses don't update, and users complete a flow that doesn't actually register on the other side. This type of rescue identifies the specific failure modes that only surface under real conditions – webhook handling, race conditions, edge cases in cancellation and modification flows – and fixes them without rebuilding the entire product.

The product was built quickly with AI assistance – Cursor, Claude Code, or similar tools. It demonstrated well. In production, edge cases fail, the architecture has gaps nobody fully understands, and the team is reluctant to change anything the AI generated because they can't predict what it will affect. AI code stabilization isn't about rewriting what the AI produced. It's about taking ownership of it: understanding what it does, filling the gaps in error handling and architecture, and making it safe to develop further.

A previous team handed over a product that works but can't be explained. Documentation is incomplete. Some integrations are unclear. The new team is afraid to touch anything. Post-handover recovery starts with mapping what exists – what each part of the product does, what the integrations connect to, and which areas are stable versus fragile. From there, the most critical gaps are filled: missing documentation, unclear ownership, and the parts of the codebase that need to be understood before they can be safely changed.

Every deployment is an event. The team is nervous before it goes out. Something unexpected happens more often than not. Hot fixes follow releases regularly. Release stabilization addresses why deployments are unpredictable – usually a combination of no visibility into what changed, no separation between stable and fragile parts of the codebase, and no rollback plan.

When something is clearly wrong with a product, the instinct is often to propose a full rebuild. It feels clean. It feels like starting fresh without the baggage.

Most of the time, a full rebuild is the wrong answer – not because it's impossible, but because it's slower, riskier, and more expensive than it looks. Existing products contain years of business logic, edge cases, and data that can't be replicated by starting over. As HackerNoon has covered in depth in pieces on technical debt, deferred structural work compounds in ways that aren't always visible until they become critical. A rebuild that takes six months to produce something equivalent to what already exists is rarely the right investment.

The right intervention depends on what's actually broken.

Stabilization is the right answer when the product's core architecture is sound but specific areas are fragile – a sync job that fails silently, an integration that breaks under certain conditions, a flow that works in testing and fails in production. Stabilization fixes those specific areas without touching what works. It's the fastest path to a safer product and the starting point for most rescue engagements.

Refactoring is the right answer when the structure of the code – not just specific bugs – is what makes development slow and risky. Modules that are too tightly coupled, logic that lives in the wrong layer, architecture decisions made early that don't fit where the product is now. Refactoring restructures without rebuilding – the product keeps running while the internal structure improves.

A full rebuild is justified when the existing codebase genuinely cannot support what the product needs to do next. Not "it's messy" or "we'd build it differently now" – those are almost always arguments for refactoring, not a rebuild. A rebuild makes sense when the technology is no longer viable, when the architecture is fundamentally incompatible with the product's requirements, or when the accumulated technical debt has made the codebase more expensive to maintain than to replace.

The practical test: if the product can be made safe to develop with targeted fixes, stabilization or refactoring is the answer. If it genuinely can't – if the architecture itself is the blocker – then a rebuild conversation is warranted.

Rescue engagements follow the same sequence regardless of which type applies.

Audit first. Before any code changes, map what exists: what's stable, what's fragile, what's blocking development, and what the highest-risk areas are. This is what determines the scope – not assumptions made before looking at the actual product.

Fix what affects users and revenue first. Not every problem needs to be solved at once. The first phase addresses the issues that are causing real impact: flows that fail, integrations that lose data, releases that create incidents. Everything else is prioritized based on risk and effort.

Stabilize, then improve. The goal of software project rescue isn't a perfect codebase – it's a product that's safe to develop. Once the critical areas are stable, refactoring and improvement can happen incrementally, without the pressure of firefighting.

Hand over with clarity. The end of a rescue engagement should leave the team with a clear picture of what changed, what to monitor, and what to address next. Not a black box – a product the team can own.

We talked a lot about the process, so here is a direct example from ASD Team’s work:

One platform connected three AI services – a language model, a text-to-speech provider, and an AI avatar tool – to turn user text into finished videos. Each service worked correctly in isolation. Together, they couldn’t complete a single video reliably.

The problem wasn’t the AI calls. It was the handoffs between them. The language model returned output that was too large and unstructured for the text-to-speech service, which needed a short script and a delivery tone. Nothing in the system performed that translation – the integrations existed, but the connection layer between them didn’t.

The team mapped each handoff, built the missing orchestration layer, removed workarounds that had accumulated around the gaps, and replaced providers that proved unstable once the full sequence ran end-to-end. The result of software project rescue services was a pipeline that completed consistently for every request.

The right time to start is before the situation becomes critical – not after a production incident forces the decision.

If development is getting slower, releases feel riskier, or specific parts of the product are avoided because nobody is confident about what changing them will affect – those are the signals. Waiting until something breaks completely doesn't make the engagement easier. It makes it more urgent, more expensive, and more disruptive.

The goal of rescue isn't a perfect codebase. It's a product that's safe to develop – where the team understands what's stable, what's fragile, and what to watch. That's the state from which normal development can resume.

#9593. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.
